newsitem.title: USA: USW makes minor progress with WHX Corp.
newsitem.headline: USW makes minor progress with WHX Corp.

text.p: The United Steelworkers union reached agreement on a minor health insurance issue with WHX Corp, against which it has been on strike since October, but no progress has been made on the major divisive issue of pensions, union officials said Wednesday.

Jim Bowen, the union's chief negotiator with WHX, said the two sides reached agreement on insurance rates for approximately 700 workers who are covered by a COBRA health plan. A COBRA plan covers a worker temporarily after he leaves an employer, before benefits of a new employer take effect.

WHX agreed to not raise premiums for the first three months of 1997, Bowen told reporters at a news conference. After that, the two sides will determine whether an increase is necessary. Premiums were scheduled to increase on January 1 had an agreement not been reached.
Despite a meeting in Pittsburgh on Tuesday between the two sides and a federal mediator, no progress has been made on the major sticking point of pensions, Bowen said.
"We met for 90 minutes and discussed numerous issues," he said. "If you had to rank the issues I would agree that pensions are number one."
WHX has maintained it cannot afford a defined benefit plan and has offered to enhance the defined contribution plan.

"As long as (WHX) will provide a (defined benefit plan)...and will provide (plant shutdown) benefits, we can resolve this matter," Bowen said. "I believe the company can afford these things for our people."

In a statement, Dan Keaton, WHX's vice president of human resources, said of Tuesday's meeting: "There was frank discussion of the issues but regrettably, the (USW) did not move at all from the position they have held regarding pensions since early September."
Bowen said no further meetings are scheduled.

Tuesday's meeting marked the first time the two sides have met since about 4,500 workers struck the company on October 1 after their former contract expired. The labor dispute centers primarily around pensions.

The union wants WHX to establish a defined benefit plan, which is funded regardless of hours worked. Workers currently have a defined contribution plan, which is funded based on age and hours worked and is generally cheaper to fund.
The strike has idled eight steel plants in three states.
